text:
PhaseNet via SeisBench, run on continuous waveforms downloaded from EarthScope, GEOFON, and Raspberry Shake FDSN. Code lives in ~/Documents/bransfield-eq/ .
| Network | Stations | Data center | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| ZX | 14 ( BRA13 – BRA27 ) | EarthScope | BRAVOSEIS OBS, low-gain ?L? |
| ZX | 8 ( BRA02–05, 08–11 ) | GEOFON ( GFZ ) | BRAVOSEIS OBS, high-gain BB HH? @ 100 Hz |
| 5M | 14 (Bransfield bbox) | GEOFON ( GFZ ) | reused temp code — bbox filter |
| AI.JUBA | 1 | EarthScope | Antarctic permanent |
| AM.R4DE2 | 1 | Raspberry Shake | bbox filter (epochs reused) |
[!warning] BRAVOSEIS OBS split across two data centers — and two instrument types
EarthScope (BRA13-27) hosts low-gain seismometers with mixed sample rates (200 Hz Z, 100 Hz horizontals, 200 Hz hydrophone).
GEOFON (BRA02-11) hosts high-gain broadband at uniform 100 Hz ( HHZ/HH1/HH2 ).
Picker handles both — resamples to 100 Hz before PhaseNet — but discrimination/location may need to treat them separately for noise floor reasons.
Window: 2019-01-01 → 2020-03-01 (BRAVOSEIS deployment + a 2-month tail).
Bbox (Bransfield): lat -65 to -60, lon -65 to -54.
The BRAVOSEIS OBS uses low-gain seismometer code, not high-gain. Initial channel filter EH?,HH?,BH?,SH? returned zero for ZX. Actual ZX seismic channels:
ELZ @ 200 Hz — short-period low-gain vertical
SL1 , SL2 @ 100 Hz — short-period low-gain horizontals
EDH @ 200 Hz — hydrophone (skipped for picking)
Final channel glob (covers all our targets):
EH?,HH?,BH?,SH?,EL?,HL?,BL?,SL?
[!warning] Sample-rate mismatch on ZX
Vertical is 200 Hz, horizontals are 100 Hz on the same station. PhaseNet expects 3C aligned at one sample rate (default 100 Hz). Plan: downsample Z to 100 Hz at picking time (SeisBench does this if you set sampling_rate=100 ), but verify on a single trace first.

sectionTitle: Disk-space budget — how it was derived
sectionPath: Disk-space budget — how it was derived
text:
Estimate uses actual operational overlap of each channel-epoch with the window, multiplied by the channel's sample rate, then divided by a Steim2 compression ratio of 3.5.
bytes_in_window = sample_rate_hz * 4 * overlap_seconds / 3.5
Initial naïve estimate (every channel-epoch × full year) gave ~2 TB and was wrong because:
ZX BRA* filter was needed — the unfiltered ZX network spans 2003-2022 and includes a New Zealand deployment in 2021/2022.
Channel-epochs are short snippets (response changes), not deployment-long.
5M includes European stations under the same temp code.
Channel filter excludes SOH ( ACE , LCE , LCQ , ...) and hydrophone.
Final estimate (seismic 3C + hydrophone, BRAVOSEIS window, all filters applied):
| Net | Stations | GB |
|---|---|---|
| ZX (EarthScope, 14 stations + GEOFON, 8 stations) | 22 | 460 (incl. hydrophone on EarthScope subset) |
| 5M | 14 | 85 |
| AI | 1 | 15 |
| AM (R4DE2) | 1 | 0.1 (only 5 days of true Bransfield data) |
| Total | 38 | ~560 GB |
Budget ~1.4 TB free disk (2.5× for raw + working copies + pick CSVs). Laptop can't host this — running on a cluster with a scratch volume.
| Network | Client |
|---|---|
| ZX, AI | Client("EARTHSCOPE") |
| 5M | Client("GFZ") (GEOFON) |
| AM | Client("https://data.raspberryshake.org") |
EarthScope token / authentication: assumed pre-configured on the run machine. Not yet tested for embargo on ZX — if download fails for ZX , that's the first thing to check.

scripts/02_download_waveforms.py :
One MSEED file per (station, day). Idempotent — file existence = "done".
Empty days written as 0-byte sentinel so 204 responses aren't retried forever.
--shard I --of N partitions the (station × day) Cartesian product across N workers — drop into a SLURM array job.
Per-channel bulk request expands the channel glob server-side.
3 retries with 10 s backoff for transient FDSN failures.
scripts/03_run_phasenet.py :
SeisBench PhaseNet with pretrained weights (start with stead ; cross-check with instance and ethz ).
Per station-day file: read → merge gaps → resample to 100 Hz → model.classify(stream) → write picks CSV.
Parameters to tune: P_threshold , S_threshold (defaults 0.3 / 0.3), blinding , overlap .
Outputs: time, station, network, phase, prob, model_weights .

instance weights (trained on European OBS data) outperform stead (land-only) substantially on Bransfield OBS. Both recall and precision improved — domain match is the right lever, not threshold-tuning alone. Defaults locked in 03_run_phasenet.py and slurm/pick.sbatch .

Download: 1.66 GB MSEED.

sectionTitle: PhaseNet caught a second event at +24 s — validation win
sectionPath: PhaseNet caught a second event at +24 s — validation win
text:
[!note] Not necessarily an "aftershock"
Earlier framing called this an aftershock; without magnitudes or locations that's overclaiming. More likely swarm pair for Bransfield's rift+volcanic context. Pin down via Stage 4 magnitudes + locations + waveform CC.
A 4-station cluster fired at 23:51:34–36 (~25 s after the 23:51:10 manual event 2 on Dec 26):
| Station | P | S | S-P |
|---|---|---|---|
| BRA19 | 23:51:34.74 | 23:51:35.33 | 0.59 s |
| BRA21 | 23:51:35.03 | — | — |
| BRA22 | 23:51:35.27 | 23:51:36.11 | 0.84 s |
| BRA20 | 23:51:35.96 | 23:51:36.02 | 0.06 s ⚠ spurious S |
S-P times of 0.6–0.8 s on BRA19/BRA22 are consistent with a local source ~5 km away — same order as event 2's BRA20 S-P of 0.98 s. Two separate events , close in time and space; not coda of event 2 (24 s gap is far too long for a local source).
Significance:
Genuine event the manual analyst either missed or merged with event 2 — demonstrates the value of running PhaseNet over the full record, not just QA against a manual catalog.
4 stations × right at PyOcto's typical association minimum → would be picked up downstream as a distinct event. Won't be lost.
instance
 weights are 
less
 confident than 
stead
 was on this borderline event (BRA19 P prob 0.97 → 0.34). For marginal events, an ensemble of stead + instance may add real signal. Revisit if Stage 2 / Stage 3 see many borderline events.

Idempotent: skip-if-exists at file granularity (MSEED for downloads, CSV for picks). Configuration consolidated in configs/targets.yaml so window/channels/targets aren't duplicated across scripts. Resampling decision: pick at 100 Hz (PhaseNet default). 200 Hz channels (ZX ELZ , EDH ) are downsampled in the picker via tr.resample(100) . This avoids the 200/100 Hz cross-component mismatch on ZX OBS but means we lose high-frequency content on the vertical — flag this if local micro-events are missed.

Station geometry extracted with scripts/04_station_geometry.py → catalogs/station_geometry.csv . BRAVOSEIS OBS sit at 1019–1495 m water depth; StationXML elevation is reliably negative for OBS, so we have water depth without GEBCO. Land stations have elevation ≥ 0.
AM.R4DE2 epoch trap (resolved) — R4DE2 is a single Raspberry Shake station code that has been physically relocated multiple times. Within our 2019-01 → 2020-03 window it has three epochs: Uruguay (2019-08 to 2020-01-20), Bransfield (2020-01-20 to 2020-01-23, ~3 days at -62.18°/-58.89°), Uruguay again (2020-01-23 to 2020-02-18), Bransfield again (2020-02-18 to 2020-02-20, ~2 days). Solution: enabled bbox_filter: true for AM in targets.yaml . The Raspberry Shake FDSN server filters by channel-epoch coordinates, so only the ~5 days of Bransfield data are returned (~0.1 GB). After 2020-08 R4DE2 has been continuously in Bransfield through 2025; if we ever extend the window past Mar 2020 we get years of permanent Raspberry Shake data .
Refactored 01_data_inventory.py to read from configs/targets.yaml so window/channels/bbox aren't duplicated across scripts. 04_station_geometry.py reads StationXML written by 01_* and adds water_depth_m for OBS.

Multi-class classification of the Stage 1 pick stream. Bransfield Basin sits at an active spreading rift adjacent to glaciated landmasses (Antarctic Peninsula, South Shetland Islands), so non-tectonic seismicity is abundant and scientifically interesting . We catalog both tectonic earthquakes and icequakes; we drop everything else.
| Class | Catalog? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| tectonic | ✅ keep, primary catalog | Local + regional EQs; the Stage 3-6 inputs |
| icequake | ✅ keep, separate catalog | Calving, basal slip, ice-shelf flexure, glacial tremor |
| ship | ✗ drop | Hydrophone-dominant transients during shipping passes |
| whale | ✗ drop | Fin/blue whale calls (15-30 Hz, repeating patterns) |
| t_phase | ✗ drop | Distant teleseismic energy via SOFAR |
| volcanic_tremor | ✗ drop (Stage 6 may revisit) | Sustained harmonic near Orca submarine volcano |
| active_source | ✗ drop | Wei's airgun shots (future); known shot times mask |
[!note] Cryoseismology context
Antarctic Peninsula has substantial cryoseismic literature (e.g. Olinger, Aster). Cataloging icequakes feeds into ice-loss / mass-balance / glacial-dynamics studies separate from the tectonic question. Keep the methodology open enough that the icequake catalog can be analyzed independently.
Pick CSV stream from [[01-ml-picking]] ( catalogs/picks/<NET>.<STA>/*.csv ).
Continuous waveforms (already on disk; need 3C seismic + hydrophone).
Optional: shot log from BRAVOSEIS / Wei active source for hard masking.
Manual ground truth from [[manual_picks]] for the tectonic class.
These are the signal-domain features for the classifier; ranked roughly by usefulness for our OBS-heavy network.
Onset gradient — sharp impulsive (EQ) vs gradual emergent (icequake). Easy to compute as the slope of the STA envelope around the pick.
Spectral centroid + bandwidth — calving and basal stick-slip usually more narrow-band and lower-centroid than local tectonic EQs.
Coda Q-factor (decay rate) — ice is highly scattering + absorptive → long, slowly-decaying codas. Earthquakes decay fast.
Harmonic content — glacial tremor shows parallel bands in the spectrogram (regular harmonic stripes). So does Orca volcanic tremor — needs location to separate.
Duration / magnitude scaling — icequakes are longer for their amplitude than EQs (multi-subevent source processes).
The OBS hydrophone ( ?DH ) is the single most useful channel for cryo-vs-tectonic.
Hydrophone:seismometer amplitude ratio — Tectonic local: H ≈ Z (slightly weaker on H).
Submerged cryo (calving, iceberg break-up): H equal to or stronger than Z (acoustic coupling into water column).
T-phase / ship / whale: H dominates by 10× or more.
P-onset coherence — tectonic: P on H aligns to ~1 sample with Z. T-phase / whale / continuous noise: no coherent P.
Bubble pulses / repeating coda on H — strong tell for iceberg disintegration / calving events.
S-P time — very short (<2 s) for surface-source cryo at ice margins.
Apparent depth — cryo locates near 0 km; Bransfield tectonic at 5-25 km. Becomes the cleanest discriminator once [[04-location]] runs, but it's a feedback, not an input feature.
Engineered features (~10 per pick): centroid, bandwidth, coda Q, H:Z ratio, P-onset coherence, onset slope, harmonic-stripe energy, S-P time, duration. Interpretable; feeds a gradient-boosted-tree classifier.
Spectrogram CNN in parallel: 2-D spectrogram window around each pick → CNN → class. Transfer-learn from published Antarctic cryo classifiers (PNSN cryo, Olinger/Aster work) rather than from scratch.
Vote between the two. Disagreement → flag for manual review + add to training-set queue. Keeps the loop going.
Shot-time masking (deterministic) — exclude picks within ±N s of known shot times.
Per-pick spectral / polarization features — used both for rule-based classes and as ML inputs: Dominant frequency, bandwidth, spectral centroid (T-phases vs EQs vs whales)
Rectilinearity / planarity (P-wave linearity)
Hydrophone-to-seismometer ratio (T-phase, ship, whale tells)
Duration / coda shape (icequakes are typically emergent + long-coda)
Time-of-day / inter-event interval (whale calls cluster; ships are continuous)
ML classifier on a short window around each pick — start with a published architecture (DiTing-style or simple CNN on spectrograms); train on labeled examples.
Post-association sanity — events that don't locate plausibly with [[03-association]] flag for re-classification.
[!note] Order matters — cheap-first cascade
Shot mask → spectral rules → ML → post-association sanity. Cheap filters first reduce ML inference cost.
Tectonic positives: manual picks from [[manual_picks]] (58k+).
Icequake positives: need labeled examples. Options: Hand-label a few hundred from the BRAVOSEIS waveforms (look for emergent onsets near the ice shelf).
Use any existing cryo-event catalogs from BRAVOSEIS or other Antarctic projects.
Bootstrap: train on tectonic-only first, then iterate on rejected picks to find icequake clusters.
Ship/whale/T-phase negatives: can often be auto-labeled with rules (high hydrophone:seismometer ratio + spectral signature) before any ML.
catalogs/picks_classified.csv — every Stage 1 pick with: class , class_prob , feature_* columns.
catalogs/picks_tectonic.csv — filtered to class == "tectonic" , schema-compatible with [[03-association]].
catalogs/picks_icequake.csv — filtered to class == "icequake" , schema as above for an icequake-specific Stage 3 run.
Stage 2 also closes a gap in [[manual_picks]] validation: once classification is in place, FP attribution from scripts/05_validate_picks.py can be split into
FP_tectonic — PhaseNet pick, classed as tectonic, no manual match. Real model error.
FP_icequake — PhaseNet pick, classed as icequake. Expected; counts toward icequake catalog instead.
FP_other — non-seismic noise. Drop silently.
This is the headline precision metric for Stage 1 sign-off. Until Stage 2 exists, use --event-window mode in the validator to avoid penalizing PhaseNet for finding icequakes/whales/ships.
Distant calving loses high-frequency content; spectrum starts to look like a distant tectonic EQ. Need location (depth → 0 km vs 5-25 km) to break the tie.
Orca volcanic tremor and glacial tremor are nearly identical in spectrum — both harmonic narrow-band. Separation is by location (Orca at -62.45° lat -58.45° lon vs ice margins at the basin's north/south coasts), not signal alone.
Boundary events (hybrid cryo-tectonic, slow-slip, ice-quake-triggered earthquakes) will exist; the classifier will return mass on both classes. Treat as a separate "uncertain" bin and human-review.

Locked stack:
PyOcto (Stage 3 association, coarse hypocenters)
 ↓
NLLoc — absolute locations ← user has this set up already with Orca 3D + 1D

Waveform cross-correlation differential times (sub-sample)

GrowClust — relative relocation, tight clusters

Run the full stack twice : once for the tectonic class from [[02-discrimination]], once for the icequake class. Different velocity priors, different depth priors, separate output catalogs.
Sparse + azimuthally biased network demands probabilistic absolute locations (NLLoc oct-tree gives PDFs, not point estimates).
Deep OBS (1019–1943 m water) require explicit water-layer travel-time corrections — already in catalogs/station_geometry.csv .
ML pick outliers on OBS make GrowClust the safer first-pass DD method (median-based, robust to bad CC pairs) over HypoDD (LSQR sensitive to outliers).
Dense rift cluster + Orca volcano benefit from the user's existing 3D blended velocity model in NLLoc.
Two seismicity classes in one dataset require class-aware depth priors: cryo near 0 km, tectonic at 5–25 km.
[!important] User has the NLLoc setup written
Existing config + 3D velocity model + 1D background. Bring it in at Stage 4 — do not rewrite from scratch. Confirm format and station-file compatibility with our catalogs/station_geometry.csv before running.
To clarify when we get there:
3D velocity model file format (and converter, if needed, for NLLoc grid format).
Coordinate system / projection / origin lat/lon of the 3D grid.
Vp/Vs assumption — model is Vp-only; need a Vp/Vs ratio to generate S travel-times. Typical for our crustal context: ~1.78. Verify against any published Bransfield S-wave studies.
1D background model file (user will provide; lives in data/velocity_models/ ).
Station file: convert catalogs/station_geometry.csv → NLLoc station list (lat, lon, elev — using our water_depth_m to get the seafloor sensor elevations correctly).
Depth prior — class-aware: tectonic 5–25 km, icequake 0–2 km. Encoded in NLLoc with LOCSEARCH OCT constraints + LOCMETH priors.
This step sits between NLLoc and GrowClust. It produces sub-sample-precision differential times from waveform similarity — and is the single biggest accuracy lever in the whole pipeline.
For each event pair within ~5 km of each other, cut a window around each P (and S) arrival, cross-correlate, take the lag at peak coherence.
Tools: lassie , EQcorrscan , or a custom ObsPy-based loop. EQcorrscan is the most popular for spreading-axis catalogs.
Output: catalogs/dt_cc.txt — GrowClust- and HypoDD-compatible format.
[!note] Worth as much engineering as the locator
Catalog-only DD (NLLoc-pick-time differences) gives ~100 m relative precision. CC-DD gets to ~10 m. Don't skip the CC step.
Inputs: NLLoc absolute hypocenters + dt_cc.txt + station file + 1D model (or 3D extracted to a 1D-per-station table).
Hierarchical cluster tree, median-robust, native QC flags per event.
Output: catalogs/events_growclust.csv with new lat/lon/depth + cluster IDs + quality flags.
Same DD math as HypoDD but with 3D ray tracing. Use the same Orca 3D + 1D blended model as NLLoc.
Run on a curated high-quality subset (well-recorded, low-residual events from 4a).
Compare GrowClust vs tomoDD locations on the same events. Agreement → publishable.

These are now in [[01-ml-picking]] but worth surfacing here as the day's "discoveries":
ZX OBS use low-gain seismometer code ( ?L? ), not high-gain ( ?H? ). Initial channel filter EH?,HH?,BH?,SH? returned zero for ZX. Real channels: ELZ @ 200 Hz vertical, SL1 / SL2 @ 100 Hz horizontals, EDH @ 200 Hz hydrophone.
ZX is a reused temp network code spanning 2003–2022 across multiple deployments (Bransfield 2019, New Zealand 2021/2022, China, UK, Costa Rica). Filter to BRA* station glob + 2019-01 → 2020-03 window.
5M is also reused — bbox filter to Bransfield, since the same code includes European stations.
R4DE2 epoch trap — the same Raspberry Shake station code has bounced between Uruguay and Bransfield several times. FDSN bbox filter at the channel-epoch level (Raspberry Shake supports it) drops the Uruguay epochs cleanly. Within our window, only ~5 days of true Bransfield data; after 2020-08 it's continuous through 2025 if we ever extend the window.
OBS water depth comes free from StationXML — elevation field is negative for seafloor sensors. GEBCO not needed for Stage 1; only for 3D ray paths in Stage 4.
Mixed sample rates within a single ZX station (200 Hz vertical, 100 Hz horizontals). Picker resamples Z to 100 Hz before PhaseNet.
Three files dropped in data/manual_picks/ : two NLLoc obs ( nllmaleen_*.out ) + one Nordic / SeisAn ( collect_regional.out ).
Parsed to canonical schema → catalogs/manual_picks.csv . 58,630 picks across 6,970 events.
Two parser quirks captured: Nordic packs station+component without whitespace (need fixed-column slicing); magnitude regex needs the last match per line, bounded to plausible range.
One mystery flagged: BRA05 appears in manual picks (239 times) but not in our FDSN-resolved inventory.
User pointed out that BRA05 is on GEOFON, not EarthScope. Cross-checking revealed 8 additional BRAVOSEIS OBS stations hosted at GEOFON: BRA02, 03, 04, 05, 08, 09, 10, 11. Total deployment = 22 OBS, with no overlap between the two data centers. Missing: BRA01, 06, 07, 12, 17 (assumed failed deployments).
The GEOFON-hosted OBS use a different instrument type — high-gain broadband at uniform 100 Hz ( HHZ/HH1/HH2 ), vs. the EarthScope-hosted low-gain mixed-rate stations. Both work with PhaseNet (resampled to 100 Hz) but downstream discrimination/location may need to treat them separately.
Inventory bumped: 560 GB total / 1.4 TB recommended free disk (was 435 GB / 1.1 TB).
Config now has two ZX targets (one per data center). Fixed a bug where both targets wrote to the same ZX_BRAALL.xml — now suffixed with data center.
Built the missing pieces so PhaseNet output can be measured against manual ground truth as soon as it exists:
manual_picks.resolve_networks() joins picks against station_geometry.csv to fill in network codes (NLLoc/Nordic don't carry them). 58,606 / 58,630 picks resolved; only ESPZ + OHG (24 picks, Antarctic regional stations outside our targets) stay blank.
scripts/05_validate_picks.py — greedy nearest-time matcher. For each (network, station, phase) reports TP/FP/FN, precision, recall, F1, residual mean/std. Defaults: P ±0.5 s, S ±1.0 s. Writes catalogs/validation_report.csv (per net × sta × phase) and catalogs/validation_per_pick.csv (per-pick, including residuals). Handles empty PhaseNet directory.
User flagged that icequakes are a research target , not just noise. Reshaped Stage 2 from binary "filter to tectonic" to multi-class classification :
Keep + catalog: tectonic, icequake (two parallel output catalogs)
Drop: ships, whales, T-phases, volcanic tremor (Orca), active-source shots
Output structure: picks_classified.csv (every pick with class + features), picks_tectonic.csv and picks_icequake.csv (split outputs that feed parallel Stage 3 association runs).
Implication: hydrophone download (already enabled) is now load-bearing — needed for ship/whale/T-phase discrimination and for cryoseismic feature extraction. Also needs labeled icequake examples for training.
This also closes the validation loop properly: once Stage 2 exists, Stage 1 FP attribution splits into FP_tectonic (real model error), FP_icequake (counts toward icequake catalog), and FP_other (silent drop).

Discussed associators and locators in detail:
Associator: PyOcto (Münchmeyer, same author as SeisBench). SeisBench itself doesn't include an associator; PyOcto is the natural pairing — fast octree search, robust to ML pick noise, drops in directly. GaMMA reserved for a 1-week sanity cross-check.
Locator stack: PyOcto → NLLoc → waveform CC → GrowClust → tomoDD (optional) . NLLoc gives PDFs (essential for our sparse, azimuthally biased network). GrowClust chosen over HypoDD as primary DD because median-based solver is more robust to ML pick outliers. tomoDD on a curated subset for cross-validation.
Velocity model: user has an Orca 3D blended with a 1D background, and an existing NLLoc setup using it. Bring it in at Stage 4 — do not rewrite. Vp only; will use Vp/Vs ≈ 1.78 for S travel-times. User will provide the 1D background model file.
Run the full Stage 3-4 stack twice — once for tectonic, once for icequake — with different velocity priors and depth ranges.
Cross-correlation step between NLLoc and GrowClust is the biggest precision lever (catalog-only DD: ~100 m, CC-DD: ~10 m). Use EQcorrscan or similar.
Stage 3 + 4 vault notes updated with the locked stack.

Ran the full Stage 1 workflow on one day to validate before cluster commitment.
Download ( 02_download_waveforms.py --start 2019-12-26 --end 2019-12-27 ):
35 / 37 stations returned data (R4DE2 correctly excluded — Uruguay epoch on this date).
1.66 GB total (~2× initial estimate; reasonable with hydrophone + GEOFON OBS included).
Picking ( 03_run_phasenet.py ):
CPU on M-series Mac, 17 min for 35 station-days.
Peak RAM 3.1 GB (PhaseNet activations + ObsPy stream).
Wall time scales linearly: full year × 38 stations ≈ 135 hours sequential, ~17 hours with an 8-way SLURM array, ~2 hours with GPU.
Validation against manual picks (Dec 26 has 23 unique manual picks across 2 events; required dedup since mag07 ⊂ magall was double-counting):
| Setting | Stations w/ picks | ML picks | P recall | S recall | P prec (event-window) | S prec (event-window) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| stead @ 0.3 | 32 | 2,068 | 9% (1/11) | 17% (2/12) | 33% | 33% |
| instance
 @ 0.2 | 35 | 3,307 | 45% (5/11) | 42% (5/12) | 38% | 63% |
Both recall AND precision up — the rare double win. Default switched in 03_run_phasenet.py and slurm/pick.sbatch to instance weights @ threshold 0.2. STEAD is land-only training data; instance was trained on European OBS, much closer to BRAVOSEIS domain.
Why recall isn't higher yet: PhaseNet still picks events on a different subset of stations than the manual analyst — for the 13:43:42 event, manual used BRA14/16/19/20/21/22/25 and PhaseNet used BRA05/13/14/15/16/18. Only BRA14 + BRA16 overlap. Doesn't matter for association (PyOcto only needs ≥4 stations), but limits per-station validation. Future fine-tuning on Bransfield manual picks should close more of the gap.

sectionTitle: PhaseNet caught a missed event at 23:51:34 — validation win
sectionPath: PhaseNet caught a missed event at 23:51:34 — validation win
text:
While inspecting Dec 26 results, a 4-station cluster surfaced at 23:51:34–36 , ~24 s after manual event 2 (23:51:10). PhaseNet picks at BRA19/BRA21/BRA22/BRA20 with S-P times of 0.6–0.8 s on the cleanest stations — a real, second local seismic event the manual analyst either missed or merged with event 2 . Not coda of event 2 (24 s gap is far too long for a local source).
[!warning] Don't call this an "aftershock" yet
Earlier draft labeled this as an aftershock — that overclaimed. We don't have magnitudes or locations yet, so the physical relationship between the two events is unconstrained. Better-supported labels for a Bransfield rift+volcanic context: Earthquake swarm pair (most likely; characteristic of spreading axes and volcanic regions)
Doublet/multiplet on the same fault patch
Triggered seismicity (static or dynamic stress transfer)
Aftershock if event 1 turns out to be larger
Foreshock–mainshock if event 2 is larger Pinning it down needs Stage 4 magnitudes + locations + waveform CC between the two.
Notes:
Borderline confidence under instance weights (BRA19 P prob 0.34 vs 0.97 with stead ). Suggests an ensemble may help on marginal events.
4 stations is right at PyOcto's typical association minimum — won't be lost downstream.
This is exactly the upside of running an ML picker over the full record: catalog-completeness gain, not just QA against the existing catalog.
Captured in [[01-ml-picking]] under "PhaseNet caught a missed event at +25 s".
Re-ran Dec 26 picks with instance @ 0.1 (down from 0.2):
| Setting | ML picks | P recall | S recall | P prec (EW) | S prec (EW) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| stead @ 0.3 | 2,068 | 9% | 17% | 33% | 33% |
| instance @ 0.2 | 3,307 | 45% | 42% | 38% | 63% |
| instance
 @ 0.1 | 6,902 | 64% | 42% | 47% | 63% |
P recall jumped 45 → 64 % with precision also up (rare double win). S recall flat — bounded by something other than threshold (likely OBS horizontals being noisier on small events). instance @ 0.1
 locked as the new default. Defaults updated in 03_run_phasenet.py and slurm/pick.sbatch .
Ran EQT @ instance @ 0.1 on Dec 26 (same data, separate output dir catalogs/picks_eqt_instance/ ):
| Model | Total picks | P | S | P recall | S recall | P prec (EW) | S prec (EW) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PhaseNet | 6,902 | 5,809 | 1,093 | 64% | 42% | 47% | 63% |
| EQTransformer | 7,126 | 5,939 | 1,187 | 36% | 50% | 31% | 67% |
Mixed result, complementary strengths:
PhaseNet wins on P (U-Net excels at sharp impulsive arrivals).
EQT wins on S (transformer + LSTM better for variable-character S onsets).
Recommendation: run both on the cluster (cheap on GPU); union of picks → PyOcto handles overlap during association. Coded --model and --out-subdir flags in 03_run_phasenet.py to support side-by-side runs.
Read [[srl-2024086.1.pdf]] (Wang, Waldhauser, Schaff, Tolstoy, Wilcock, Tan — "Real-Time Detection of Volcanic Unrest and Eruption at Axial Seamount Using Machine Learning"). Their stack:
PhaseNet → GaMMA → NLLoc → HypoDD + waveform CC → SpecUFEx (unsupervised classification)
+ 30-50/4-50 Hz freq-ratio rule for fin-whale calls
+ 15s overlapping windows in real-time (6s during high seismicity)
Validates our locked stack almost component-for-component. Things to adopt:
SpecUFEx unsupervised feature clustering for [[02-discrimination]] — alternative or complement to our planned supervised CNN.
Whale-call frequency ratio rule (30–50 / 4–50 Hz energy) — drop-in deterministic discriminator.
1 s pre-P + 3 s post-P spectrogram window for classification features — adopt as default.
PhaseNet pick std on OBS : 17 ms (P), 40/28 ms (S) — useful prior for our CC differential-time uncertainty.
Self-training (Yarowsky) for label reconciliation across stations — useful pattern for class-aware FP attribution.
What we do that they don't: explicit hydrophone features, manual analyst picks as direct ground truth. Their training data was Kurtosis-picked baseline.
User has a free 32-CPU 128-GB cluster, with options including a Pytorch instance (32 CPU + 187 GB + 1 GPU) . Decision: use Pytorch from the start since GPUs are free. Single-instance workflow:
Setup: 5 min
Verify on 1 day with --device cuda : ~5 min
Full year download: ~2-3 h (FDSN-bound, GPU idle)
Full year picking on GPU: ~30-60 min (vs 17 h on 32 CPUs)
Validation: <1 min
If both PhaseNet + EQT runs are wanted: ~2 h total picking on GPU.
Quick poor-man's associator (≥4 stations within 5s window) on PhaseNet picks for Dec 26 finds ~214 candidate event clusters . Manual catalog has only 2 events. Hourly distribution of clusters is roughly uniform — doesn't suggest dominant ship/whale (diurnal) noise contamination.
Realistic estimate after proper PyOcto association (spatial+temporal coherence): ~50-100 events , of which maybe 30-60 tectonic and 20-40 cryo after Stage 2. 15-30× catalog completeness gain vs the manual catalog for this single day.
Implication: the manual catalog is a hand-curated subset (probably triggered-detector + magnitude/quality cutoff), not a complete record. Use it as a validation set for ML accuracy on confirmed events, not as ground truth for completeness — i.e., don't treat "missing from manual" as evidence of false positive.
scripts/plot_manual_picks_day.py produces per-event waveform plots:
Solid lines = manual picks, dashed = PhaseNet, dotted = EQT ( --ml-subdirs picks,picks_eqt_instance )
Stations on each panel = union of stations with any pick (manual OR ML) within ±2 s of event window — not just analyst-picked stations
--center-time mode for plotting events with no manual entry (e.g., the 23:51:34 second event)
Output: figures/picks_<date>_<event-id>.png
Three figures generated for Dec 26 (events 1, 2, second event at +24 s) — visually confirms ML pickers track manual picks tightly when both fire, and EQT recovers some S that PhaseNet misses.
In rough priority order:
~~Investigate BRA05 ~~ — resolved (GEOFON-hosted).
~~Threshold tuning~~ — instance @ 0.1 locked.
~~Compare PhaseNet vs EQT~~ — both have strengths; run both on cluster.
Verify on cluster — Pytorch GPU instance, run 1 day end-to-end, confirm numbers match laptop.
Full-year cluster run — download (~2-3 h) + PhaseNet + EQT picking on GPU (~2 h total) + validate.
Add PyOcto association to the pipeline so we have real event counts, not pick counts.
Begin Stage 2 (multi-class classification: tectonic + icequake) — adopt SpecUFEx unsupervised clustering + whale freq-ratio rule from Wang 2024.
Pin down the 23:51:34 second event physically — magnitudes, locations, waveform CC against event 2 — once Stage 4 lands.

noteTitle: Plan — OBS noise denoiser + PhaseNet fine-tuning
sectionPath: Plan — OBS noise denoiser + PhaseNet fine-tuning
text:
The 14-month BRAVOSEIS deployment is all the data we have. The goal is an expanded earthquake catalog beyond what the manual analyst caught ( nllmaleen_mag07_202210.out — 12,099 picks across 1,126 events). The baseline picker (PhaseNet instance + OBSTransformer @ 0.5) recovered only P recall ≈ 0.42 / S recall ≈ 0.78 on Feb 4–13 — too many easy events are slipping through. The fix is two-sided: Train a DeepDenoiser on BRAVOSEIS-OBS waveforms — an STFT U-Net seisbench.models.DeepDenoiser , initialised from original weights and adapted to OBS noise. Fine-tune PhaseNet on a curated set of 30 high-density days, using the trained denoiser to (a) generate noise-mixed training variants and (b) optionally provide a "cleaned" event channel. Honest evaluation on a fully-held-out August 2019 (1,144 picks over 26 active days, 106 events). This plan refines the existing draft to align with the repo's actual conventions ( catalogs/picks// , catalogs/manual_picks.csv , --out-subdir , the existing match_one_group matcher in scripts/05_validate_picks.py ) and removes references to files that the draft assumed existed but don't ( scripts/06_* , scripts/07_* , phasenet-retrain clone). flowchart TB subgraph inputs[Inputs] WAV[data/waveforms/NET/STA/*.mseed] MAN[catalogs/manual_picks.csv

Phase 2 — 31 variants/pick] EVH --> AUG NSH --> AUG AUG --> AUGDS[(data/seisbench/bransfield_aug.h5
~100k windows)] AUGDS --> FT[09_finetune_phasenet.py
Phase 3 — Lightning fine-tune] FT --> FTCKPT[(models/phasenet_bransfield_v1/best.ckpt)] FTCKPT --> RUN[03_run_phasenet.py
--weights ckpt:<path>

File: scripts/test_deepdenoiser.py (NEW, throwaway) Load sbm.DeepDenoiser.from_pretrained('original') . Pull 3 mag07 event windows + 3 noise windows directly from data/waveforms/... using mseed_path() and the pick times from catalogs/manual_picks.csv (filter source_file contains mag07 , uncertainty_s ≤ 0.1 ). Apply denoiser via model.annotate(stream) per docs, plot original/denoised/residual to figures/dd_sanity/*.png . Decision: if denoised events look mangled (impulsive arrivals lost), retraining is required (Phase 1 is mandatory). If reasonable, retraining is still the plan but we have a cheap fallback.

sectionTitle: Phase 1 — Build OBS noise/event pools, train OBS-DeepDenoiser (~1 h GPU)
sectionPath: Plan — OBS noise denoiser + PhaseNet fine-tuning
Phase 1 — Build OBS noise/event pools, train OBS-DeepDenoiser (~1 h GPU)
text:
File: scripts/06_extract_event_noise.py (NEW)
Walk the 30 curated training days (see § Training day list ) and the
station inventory:
Event windows: for each mag07 pick with uncertainty_s ≤ 0.1 on a
curated day, cut a 30 s window around the pick from the matching
 data/waveforms/<NET>/<STA>/*.mseed . Reuse _channel_match() from
 scripts/03_run_phasenet.py for picking-channel selection. Target rate
100 Hz (matches --target-rate default), 3-channel ZNE.
Noise windows: for each curated station-day, sample candidate 30 s
windows and gate them through three filters before keeping: Manual-pick exclusion — >60 s from any pick in both 
 nllmaleen_mag07_202210.out and nllmaleen_magall_202210.out 
( magall ⊃ mag07 and catches the lower-confidence events the draft's
 mag07 -only filter would have missed).
STA/LTA detector reject — run
 obspy.signal.trigger.classic_sta_lta(tr, nsta=int(0.5*fs), nlta=int(10*fs)) 
on the candidate window's vertical channel and reject if any sample
exceeds ratio 3.0. Catches events the analyst missed and non-tectonic
transients (icequakes, whales, ships, T-phases) — exactly what the
denoiser must treat as noise, not signal.
Amplitude sanity — reject windows whose RMS is <1e-3 × the
station-day median RMS (dropouts/dead channels) or >10 × median
(clipping/spikes that aren't real noise).
Target ~500 surviving windows per curated station-day. Plot the
acceptance rate per station-day to figures/noise_qc.png so we can spot
stations with pathological selection (e.g. 5 % acceptance → station has
swarm activity outside mag07 catalog).
Write SeisBench-format datasets: data/seisbench/bransfield_events.h5 + metadata.csv
data/seisbench/bransfield_noise.h5 + metadata.csv
File: scripts/07_train_obs_denoiser.py (NEW)
DeepDenoiser is a masking STFT U-Net: given (signal + noise), it predicts
a TF mask isolating the signal. SeisBench's STFTDenoiserLabeller builds
the supervisory mask from clean signal + noise pairs.
- model = sbm.DeepDenoiser.from_pretrained('original')
- generator pipeline:
 pick random event window from bransfield_events
 pick random noise window from bransfield_noise
 mix at SNR ∈ [0.5, 10]
 STFTDenoiserLabeller -> mask
- Train: AdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 32, 50 epochs, MSE on mask
- 90/10 split by station (held-out stations validate generalisation,
 not just held-out windows of the same station)
- Save best by val_loss to models/deepdenoiser_obs/best.pt
Verify: plot 6 held-out windows pre/post denoising; val_loss curve
in figures/dd_train_loss.png .
File: scripts/08_build_augmented_dataset.py (NEW)
For each of ~3,300 high-confidence picks across the 30 curated training days
(filter source_file contains mag07 AND uncertainty_s ≤ 0.1 ):
30 noise variants: mix the event window with random noise samples
from bransfield_noise.h5 at SNR ∈ [0.5, 10].
1 denoised variant: apply the OBS-DeepDenoiser checkpoint from
Phase 1.
→ ~31 × 3,300 ≈ ~100k SeisBench-format training windows in
 data/seisbench/bransfield_aug.h5 + metadata.csv . Each row carries
per-pick P/S sample indices for PhaseNet's ProbabilisticLabeller .
The dataloader in Phase 3 layers fresh online noise mixing + temporal
jitter + channel dropout on top each epoch — pre-materialising 31 variants
is for speed, online aug for variety.
File: scripts/09_finetune_phasenet.py (NEW)
We're not vendoring phasenet-retrain as separate copies — instead,
write a single self-contained Lightning script that uses SeisBench's own
training pipeline ( sbg.GenericGenerator , sbg.WaveformDataset ,
PhaseNet's built-in forward + cross-entropy on the 3-channel
target mask). This avoids importing a third-party package and patching
its _load_custom_data() NotImplementedError stub.
Skeleton:
- model = sbm.PhaseNet.from_pretrained('instance') # transfer learning
- ds = sbd.WaveformDataset('data/seisbench/bransfield_aug')
- generator = sbg.GenericGenerator(ds)
 generator.add_augmentations([
 RandomWindow(samples=3001),
 ChangeDtype(np.float32),
 Normalize(detrend_axis=-1),
 ProbabilisticLabeller(label_columns=['P','S']),
 # online aug:
 OneOf([NoiseMix(p=0.5), GaussianNoise(p=0.3), Identity(p=0.2)]),
 ChannelDropout(p=0.1),
 ])
- Lightning Trainer: max_epochs 30, batch 64, lr 1e-4, AdamW
- Save best by val P+S F1 to models/phasenet_bransfield_v1/best.ckpt
Config: configs/phasenet_finetune.yaml (NEW) — pretrained tag,
data path, hyperparameters. Keep alongside configs/targets.yaml .

[!note] Polarities / hand-locations
Current set has P/S times + magnitudes. No polarities, no hand-located events. The schema reserves columns for them so they can be added later without a migration.
Validation: match each manual pick to the nearest PhaseNet pick on the same channel within ±0.5 s (P) / ±1.0 s (S). Compute precision/recall by station and overall.
Threshold tuning: sweep P_threshold / S_threshold over the validation set to find the operating point that matches your manual sensitivity.
Fine-tuning: if pick volume permits (≥ ~1000), fine-tune PhaseNet weights on Bransfield-specific data. Otherwise stick with stead / instance defaults.
Manual picks are assumed to be tectonic earthquakes — use them as the positive class for any ML discriminator. Need a separate negative set (T-phases, shots, ice signals).
Run associator on manual picks alone. Should cluster into the user's known events. If it doesn't, the associator config is the problem — not the picks.
If/when hand-located events arrive, compare to NLLoc / HypoDD locations as ground truth. Per-axis residual distributions (Δlat, Δlon, Δdepth, Δtime) measure absolute accuracy.
N/A unless polarities are added.

noteTitle: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
sectionPath: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
text:
Manual picks are tectonic earthquakes only; PhaseNet will (correctly) also pick non-tectonic signals that have no manual entry:
Icequakes / cryo-signals — calving, basal slip, harmonic tremor; emergent onsets
Whale calls — fin and blue whales emit 15–30 Hz calls that look like seismic transients on OBS
Ship noise — hydrophone-dominant, broadband transients during shipping passes
T-phases — late, low-frequency, hydrophone-dominant
Volcanic tremor — sustained narrow-band signals near Orca submarine volcano
Active-source shots — once Wei's airguns deploy
Naive precision = TP / (TP + FP) over-penalises PhaseNet because all of the above land in FP. Two mitigations in scripts/05_validate_picks.py :
--event-window N (cheap, available now): only count PhaseNet picks within ±N seconds of any manual event origin time. Outside those windows, PhaseNet picks are ignored — neither TP nor FP. This isolates "did we recover known earthquakes" from "what fraction of all picks are tectonic". Trade-off: doesn't measure precision over the whole record, only inside known-event windows.
Class-aware FP attribution (deferred to [[02-discrimination]]): once we have a discriminator, split FPs into "tectonic-class but no manual match" (real model error) vs "non-tectonic class" (expected, not the picker's fault).
Use mode 1 for Stage 1 sign-off. Use mode 2 as the headline metric once Stage 2 lands.

Meeting Notes data management and flow are centered on creating a streamlined, efficient pipeline for moving raw observational data into accessible public repositories like EarthScope. The discussion highlights a shift toward cloud-based processing and collaborative software development. The Data Pipeline: PI NAS to EarthScope The primary objective is to develop a protocol to move data from the PI NAS (Network Attached Storage) to EarthScope . Currently, the team views data sitting solely in the PI NAS as "functionally useless" and wants to ensure all project data, including that from "COSZO," eventually ends up in EarthScope. Test Case: The team plans to use data from Scripps SCPRs (Self-Contained Pressure Recorders) as a test case to develop these data streams. Frequency: Data transfer is intended to be daily rather than real-time. Raw vs. Calibrated Data: The strategy for EarthScope is to ingest raw data rather than derived products. The modern approach is for users to request data which is then processed into useful products "on the fly" in the cloud. Software and Technical Processing Because EarthScope will primarily host raw data, the project requires local tools to make that data useful for scientists. Python Packages: There is a plan to create a Python-based package—modeled after OBSpy —that allows users to import functions for pulling, cleaning, and applying calibrations to the data. Clock and Timing Corrections: A significant portion of the data management effort involves correcting timing jumps and data gaps. The team emphasizes the need for scripts that can handle clock jumps by setting boundaries rather than averaging data across the jump. Derived Products: Beyond pressure data, the team is looking at products for HYS4 and other short-period data requiring clock corrections. Infrastructure: GitHub and Website Migration The meeting participants expressed dissatisfaction with the current "COSZO" website, noting it "absolutely sucks" and remains "under construction". WordPress Migration: The plan is to migrate the project's public face to a WordPress site to meet disability requirements and simplify maintenance. GitHub Integration: GitHub is identified as the central hub for hosting software, Python scripts, and technical instrument documentation, such as README files explaining timing fixes. Collaborative Benefits: Using GitHub allows for collaborative development where multiple researchers can branch or fork repositories, though there were noted concerns regarding GitHub’s 100MB file size limit and the complexities of managing private versus public repositories. Based on the meeting discussion, the ring.conf file is the configuration file for the Ring server, located in the conf/ directory on the COSZO virtual machine. Key Configuration Details: The file specifies that the Ring server uses the "MiniSeed_scan" method, which: Scans the MiniSeed folder ( output/MiniSeed/ ) for new data files Loads the data into the "ring" (an in-memory buffer) Makes the data available for EarthScope's SeedLink client to retrieve How It Works: When data files are placed in the MiniSeed folder, the Ring server: Detects the new files through the scan method Loads them onto the ring buffer EarthScope's client reads from this ring and archives the data Important Note: The final line in ring.conf contains the MiniSeed_scan configuration that points to the MiniSeed folder path. This is what enables the automatic detection and transfer of pressure gauge data to EarthScope. Mika mentioned there's additional documentation about Ring server configuration in the COSZO Drive under "Non-Tier 1 Data Flow" if you need more detailed information about other settings in the file.

A new folder coszo-data-collection/testk/ was added with two standalone scripts. These are separate from the main pipeline — they don't use the shell wrappers or cron, and they write to their own output directory.
testk/pull_data.py 
Standalone script that replicates the core data request and conversion logic:
Loads OOI credentials from .ooi_env
Fetches most recent deployment info from the OOI M2M API
Submits an async 24-hour data request
Polls status.json until the job is ready (up to 10 tries, 30s apart)
Resolves the NetCDF file location via the NCML manifest
Opens the NetCDF via OPeNDAP (no download required)
Detects gaps using robust median Δt (same logic as main pipeline — [[gap detection]])
Splits time series at gaps and writes one MiniSEED file per channel per segment
Output goes to testk/output/mseed/
Reuses from main repo:
bin/read_param.py — parameter file parsing
bin/convert_utc.py — 1900-epoch timestamp conversion ( utcdata1900 )
To run:
cd coszo-data-collection
conda run -n ooi_env python testk/pull_data.py
To change the time window, edit START_TIME and END_TIME near the top of the script.
testk/verify_mseed.py 
Reads back all .mseed files in testk/output/mseed/ and:
Prints sample count, start/end times, duration, sampling rate, and data min/max/mean for each file
Generates a time-series plot saved to testk/output/verify_plot.png

conda run -n ooi_env python testk/verify_mseed.py

sectionPath: Mode 1:  collect  — Build the Metrics Library
text: Replace the current Panel 1 (sample index vs timestamp) with a histogram of timing residuals . The timestamp-vs-index plot is useful for understanding overall shape but redundant once you have the Δt panel — the histogram gives the distributional information that's actually hard to read from the scatter. New 3-panel layout: | Panel | Content | What it shows | |-------|---------|---------------| | 1 | Histogram of residuals (ms, from best-fit line) | Shape of jitter distribution: Gaussian = random noise, bimodal = quantization artifact, long tail = occasional large timing errors | | 2 | Residuals scatter (sample index vs residual in ms) | Temporal structure — drift over the day, clusters, sudden jumps | | 3 | Δt between consecutive samples with adaptive gap threshold | Gap detection, whether threshold is well-placed | Histogram details: X axis: residual in ms, centred at 0 Bin width: auto (Freedman-Diaconis or fixed ~1ms bins) Vertical lines: ±1σ, ±p95 Annotate: σ, p95, skewness, n samples Overlay a Gaussian curve fit for easy comparison The residuals scatter (Panel 2) stays because it shows when during the day the jitter occurs — the histogram alone loses that temporal information. compute_stats() must be refactored to follow this order: Step 1 — Gap detection Compute all Δt ( np.diff(t_sec) ) across the full day Estimate day-level sp_calc from the full Δt array (robust median of lower 90th percentile — resistant to large gap intervals so this still works) Apply adaptive threshold, identify gap_idx Log: n_gaps , gap locations, gap durations, estimated missing samples per gap Step 2 — Per-segment sample rates Split t_sec into contiguous segments at gap_idx For each segment: compute its own sp_calc_seg (robust median Δt within that segment) Log: segment index, duration, sample count, sample rate Detects whether segments disagree — e.g. sensor slowed down after a dropout Step 3 — Jitter metrics (per segment, then concatenated) For each segment independently: fit a line, compute residuals Compute William's metric using the segment-level sp_calc_seg as the denominator: jitter_i = |dti / sp_calc_seg - round(dti / sp_calc_seg)| Using segment-level rate matters: if two segments run at slightly different rates, measuring jitter against a blended day-level average fits neither segment correctly Concatenate residuals and jitter values across all segments Compute summary stats of the combined jitter array: jitter_mean — mean jitter_median — median (robust central tendency) jitter_std — standard deviation jitter_p95 — 95th percentile (anomaly trigger candidate) jitter_max — maximum (catches worst single interval) Compute summary stats of the combined residuals array: res_std_ms — standard deviation in ms res_p95_ms — 95th percentile in ms skewness — asymmetry (negative/positive drift within segments) Important: residuals must be computed per segment, not across the whole day. If there is a gap mid-day and the best-fit line is fitted through all samples across the gap, the line slope is distorted by the gap. Samples before the gap appear systematically early and samples after appear systematically late — the histogram shows a smeared or bimodal distribution that looks like jitter or drift

sectionPath: Mode 1:  collect  — Build the Metrics Library
text: jitter_max — maximum (catches worst single interval) Compute summary stats of the combined residuals array: res_std_ms — standard deviation in ms res_p95_ms — 95th percentile in ms skewness — asymmetry (negative/positive drift within segments) Important: residuals must be computed per segment, not across the whole day. If there is a gap mid-day and the best-fit line is fitted through all samples across the gap, the line slope is distorted by the gap. Samples before the gap appear systematically early and samples after appear systematically late — the histogram shows a smeared or bimodal distribution that looks like jitter or drift but is purely a gap artifact. Correct approach: Detect gaps first ( gap_idx already available) Split t_sec into contiguous segments at gap boundaries For each segment independently: fit a line, compute residuals Concatenate all segment residuals into one array Histogram and scatter are built from this concatenated array This ensures residuals reflect only within-segment timing irregularity. For the residuals scatter (Panel 2): colour-code points by segment so it is visually clear which residuals belong to which contiguous block. Gaps appear as breaks between colour groups.

sectionPath: Mode 1:  collect  — Build the Metrics Library
text:
For the first pass , only trigger on structural anomalies where no baseline is needed:
Any gap detected ( n_gaps > 0 )
Day is incomplete ( is_full = False )
Sample period deviation exceeds hybrid alert threshold ( sp_alert = True )
Jitter threshold is disabled on the first pass. The current code computes res_std , res_p95 , and William's jitter metric per day, but there is no meaningful threshold to compare against yet — every sensor has some baseline spread from network ingestion delays and timestamp rounding, and res_std > 0 is always true.
To establish a jitter threshold:
Run collect over a 30–60 day test window
Plot jitter p95 over time (summary Figure 3)
The distribution of values across clean days defines the normal baseline
Flag days where jitter p95 exceeds e.g. 3× the median baseline as anomalous
Set that value as jitter_p95_threshold in run_prest.txt and enable the trigger
Until Step 4 is done, jitter-based figure triggering is a guess. All jitter metrics are still stored in the CSV every day regardless — the threshold only controls whether a figure is generated.

Defined as:
jitter_i = |dti / mean_dt - round(dti / mean_dt)|
Where:
dti = inter-sample intervals ( np.diff(t_sec) )
mean_dt = sp_calc (robust median sample period, same as the pipeline uses)
Interpretation:
For a perfectly uniform signal: dti / mean_dt ≈ 1.0 for every interval → jitter ≈ 0
For a jittered signal: each interval deviates slightly from an integer multiple → jitter > 0
For a genuine gap: dti / mean_dt is a large integer (e.g. 5, 10, …) → round() cancels it → jitter ≈ 0 again
The metric is insensitive to gaps and specifically sensitive to sub-sample timing irregularity

Pressure channel only. fetch_nc_timestamps reads only the time variable from the NetCDF — never pressure or temperature values. Temperature timestamps are identical to pressure. One API call per station per day is sufficient. No code change needed.
Why calls are slow. The OOI M2M API is async:
Submit request (~instant)
Poll status.json until job completes ( max_cycle=5 , delay=50s → up to 250s wait)
Open NetCDF via OPeNDAP and read timestamps
In practice a 24h window completes in 1–2 polls ≈ 50–100s per call.
Scale estimate. 3 stations × ~4000 days = ~12,000 calls × ~90s = ~12 days wall clock. Collect must run in chunks across multiple sessions. The CSV skip logic handles this — already-processed rows are skipped on resume.

Focus: Continued revisions to diagnose_timing.py per-day figure layout and understanding of timing metrics. Builds on [[04-10-26 Notes]].
| Metric | Definition | What it tells you |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|
| sp_nominal | Fixed from param file (e.g. 1.000000 s) | What the sensor should do — never changes |
| sp_calc | Robust median of inter-sample intervals (lower 90th percentile Δt) | What the sensor typically does that day — resistant to gaps and outliers |
| sp_fit | Least-squares slope through all timestamps | Average rate across the full day — sensitive to start/end position of data |
sp_calc ≠ sp_nominal → clock running fast or slow relative to design spec
sp_fit ≠ sp_calc → interval distribution is skewed; some very short or long intervals pull the mean away from the median. Strong skewness in residuals (Panel 1) is a symptom.
sp_fit ≠ sp_nominal → overall day-level drift from nominal when integrated across the whole day
Plot sp_calc − sp_nominal , sp_fit − sp_nominal , and sp_calc − sp_fit as time series across all days in the metrics CSV. This would reveal:
Long-term clock drift — is sp_calc consistently above/below nominal over weeks/months? Would show up as a persistent offset in sp_calc − sp_nominal .
Day-to-day variability — scatter in sp_calc from day to day may indicate instrument instability or environmental effects (pressure, temperature).
Skewness signature — large sp_calc − sp_fit on a given day means the interval distribution is asymmetric. Combined with residual skewness metric, this flags days with unusual timing behaviour that isn't just clock drift.
Deployment transitions — expect a step change in sp_calc at deployment boundaries (dep1 = 15 s, dep2 = 1 s). The series should be flat within each deployment.
sp_nominal = 1.000000 s
sp_calc = 1.000502 s (+0.502 ms above nominal — clock slightly slow)
sp_fit = 1.000000 s (+0.000 ms — mean rate equals nominal for this day)
sp_calc − sp_fit = +0.502 ms — skewed distribution; median > mean
The discrepancy between sp_calc and sp_fit is the skewness signature: most intervals are 1.000502 s but enough short intervals exist to bring the day-average back to 1.000000 s. Panel 1 residuals show skewness = −3.54, confirming this.
In plot_mode Figure 1 (sample rate over time), consider adding a third scatter series for sp_fit in addition to sp_calc , with the three reference lines. Over a long time series, divergence between sp_calc and sp_fit trends would indicate changing skewness character in the data.

Replaced the old per-segment nominal residual computation with the round() approach in compute_stats() .
Old approach — anchored at each segment's first sample:
res_nominal[i] = (seg[i] - seg[0]) - i_within_seg * sp_nominal
Problem: after a gap, the next segment resets its anchor, but accumulated drift within a segment still grew without bound on long segments. Bins could blow up on gapped days.
New approach — gap-aware, anchored at first sample of the day:
t_rel = t_sec - t_sec[0]
nominal_slots = round(t_rel / sp_nominal)
res_nominal = t_rel - nominal_slots * sp_nominal
Properties:
Always bounded to ±sp_nominal/2 (e.g. ±500 ms for 1 s sampling) — no more millions-of-bins hang
Gap-aware: round() naturally skips missing nominal slots; after a gap, samples are assigned to the correct slot rather than the one immediately after the last pre-gap sample
No per-segment anchoring needed — the slot assignment is self-consistent across the full day
Panel 4 x-axis changed from sample index to nominal slot number. Because missing samples have no slot entry, gaps appear as empty horizontal regions in the scatter rather than being compressed into consecutive indices.

| green | clean | 5 | has data, no gaps, is_full=True , no sp alert — nominal day |
Priority order in the classifier: sp_alert → gaps+incomplete → gaps → incomplete → clean . A day with both a sample-rate alert and gaps will show as purple, not red.
n_points = number of samples actually in that day's file after loading/gap-splitting ( len(t_sec) ). Nothing more.
Gap splitting = within a day's timestamp array, flag intervals dt > multiplier × sp_calc as gaps ( diagnose_timing.py:448–470 ), then np.split(t_sec, gap_idx+1) partitions samples into contiguous segments. No samples are dropped — just grouped into runs separated by gaps. Used downstream for per-segment stats ( sp_seg , jitter).
expected_npts = round((data_end − data_start) / sp_calc) + 1 . Based on the observed data window, not a calendar day. Flagged as misleading for full-day coverage → that's why Figure 4 now uses 86400 / sp_nominal and 86400 / sp_fit[day] instead.

Reworked the 2×2 panel figure. Panel C (timestamps vs reconstructed index)
was removed — the OLS line always looks linear at this scale, so it added no
diagnostic value. Split the interval-count histogram into two zoomed views:
| Panel | Content |

Rationale: the old single A-panel had to span 0 to whatever the largest gap

Triggered by inspection of SLBS 2025-01-26 : the CSV said

"how can a day with a missing sample still have 86400 points?"
Added a new metric — n_ideal — defined simply as the length of the
reconstructed ideal sample index:
$$
n_{\text{ideal}} = i_{j,,\text{last}} + 1
$$
For SLBS 2025-01-26, n_ideal = 86401 .
Pushed on this and it doesn't hold up:
first sample 00:00:00.096 → last sample 23:59:59.117
wall-clock span ≈ 86399.02 s
at sp_nominal = 1.0 s , the ideal-grid slot count that physically fits
in that span is floor(86399.02 / 1.0) + 1 = 86400
we have 86400 samples → every slot is filled → no sample is
actually missing
So the n_gaps = 1, gap_total_missing = 1 is a false positive from
the rounding rule in Steps 3–4 of the plan.
dt_FG = median(Δt) = 1.000590 s for SLBS that day (larger than the true
1.0 s because of asymmetric jitter). One interval in the file is probably
≈ 1.5 s — a jitter event, not a dropout. Its normalised step count is
 Δi' = 1.5 / 1.000590 ≈ 1.499 . If that value tips just above 1.5 it
rounds to 2 (flagged as a gap); just below 1.5 it rounds to 1 (no gap).
The classifier is brittle at the Δi = 1.5 boundary.
The OLS fit confirms the grid has been stretched to absorb the fake extra
slot: Δt_true ≈ 0.999989 s (we only print 6 decimals, so it looks like
1.000000). That sub-1.0 slope lets 86401 slots fit into 86399 s.
So n_ideal = 86401 is arithmetically consistent with the reconstructed
grid but misleading as "samples the day should have held" — it
inherits the rounding artifact.

Wall-clock cross-check. Compute
 n_expected_wall = round((data_end − data_start) / sp_nominal) + 1 .
If n_points == n_expected_wall , suppress the spurious gap flag.
Tighter gap criterion. Only call it a gap when
 Δt > 1.5 × sp_nominal and Δi_int > 1 , using sp_nominal instead
of the noisy median dt_FG .
Decision pending — will pick one before re-running collect.
n_ideal = 86400 — same as n_points.
This is actually interesting and contradicts my earlier arithmetic. I was assuming n_ideal = n_points + gap_total_missing = 86401, but the actual reconstructed index length is 86400.
The explanation: somewhere in the day there's also at least one interval where Δi' rounds to 0 (two samples very close together, Δt < 0.5 × dt_FG). Those cancel the Δi = 2 event, so the net sum of Δi_j is 86399 → i_j[-1] = 86399 → n_ideal = 86400.
So the plan's rounding scheme is producing a paired artifact: one spurious "gap" (Δi=2) somewhere, paired with a spurious "overlap" (Δi=0) somewhere else. Net: no missing samples, which matches the wall-clock arithmetic. n_gaps = 1, gap_total_missing = 1 is misleading on its own — and n_ideal = 86400 is what actually tells you the day is whole.

Files land in output/temporal_anomaly/netcdf/ as <station>_<YYYY-MM-DD>_deployment<NNNN>.nc . Overwrites on re-run.

Previously collect mode always wrote a 4-panel figure on every successfully processed day.
Now with --only-gaps , the figure is only written when the post-correction n_gaps > 0 .
CSV row is always written — figure_generated column reflects whether the figure was actually produced.
Skips both cases described by William: Day with no Δi>1 events at all ( n_gaps_raw = 0 ).
Day where Δi>1 events were reclassified as jitter by the wall-clock check ( wall_clock_clean = True → n_gaps = 0 ).
# collect a date range, download NetCDFs, only plot real-gap days
python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py --mode collect \
 --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-03-31 --save-nc --only-gaps

|---|---|---|---|

The gap method in temporal_anomaly_investigator is not the same as the one in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py . Confirmed after reviewing both.
dt = np.diff(t) , strip top 10% → sp = median(dt_clean) .
Multiplier chosen by sample rate and whether segment is full: sp ≥ 10 s (15 s PREST): 3× or 4× → threshold ~45–60 s
sp ≥ 0.5 s: 2.5× or 3.5× → ~2.5–3.5 s
sp < 0.5 s: 2.0× or 2.5×
Gap = any Δt > multiplier × sp (absolute seconds).
Purpose: split MiniSEED files at gap boundaries.
Δt_FG = median(Δt') (plain median, no trim).
Δiⱼ = round(Δt'ⱼ / Δt_FG) — sample-step count.
Raw gap = any Δiⱼ > 1 .
Wall-clock correction: if n_points ≥ span/sp_nominal + 1 , reclassify all Δi>1 as jitter not gaps → n_gaps = 0 , wall_clock_clean = True .
Single missing sample ≈ 30 s. Below the pipeline's 45–60 s threshold → pipeline passes as continuous. Investigator flags n_gaps_raw = 1 , then wall-clock check decides whether real ( n_gaps = 1 ) or jitter ( n_gaps = 0 ).
Investigator is strictly more sensitive to single-sample gaps than the pipeline, with jitter discrimination on top.
n_gaps_raw , gap_total_missing_raw — pre-correction counts.
n_gaps , gap_total_missing — post-correction (the values the summary figures use and the ones --only-gaps gates on).
n_expected_wall — wall-clock threshold used for the correction.
max_abs_epsilon — rounding-stability sanity check (values near 0.5 mean Δi rounding is unstable; Δt_FG probably wrong).
Commit 6c5c5f4 on dev/maleen . Standalone tool to re-use locally saved NetCDFs without touching OOI.
Read .nc files saved by temporal_anomaly_investigator --save-nc (default output/temporal_anomaly/netcdf/ ).
Reproduce the investigator's 4-panel variability figure + variability_stats.txt without re-fetching.
Optional: convert the NetCDF to MiniSEED using the main pipeline's gap detection + per-segment split logic.
Does not read or modify the collect-mode metrics CSVs.
Figures: output/temporal_anomaly/figures_offline/<station>_<date>/ Separate from collect-mode figures/per_day/ on purpose — nothing from collect is overwritten.
MiniSEED: output/temporal_anomaly/mseed/<YEAR>/<NET>.<STA>.<LOC>.<CHA>.<start>-<end>.mseed
Imports compute_variability , make_per_day_figure , write_stats from temporal_anomaly_investigator.py , so the figure is byte-identical to what collect produces. The MiniSEED conversion mirrors the pipeline logic in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py (sample-period from trimmed-median Δt, adaptive multiplier by sp regime, split at dt > multiplier × sp , write one MiniSEED per channel × contiguous segment).
# single day, all 3 stations
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --date 2019-01-15
# range, one station, with MiniSEED conversion
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-01-07 \
 --station RS01SLBS-MJ01A-06-PRESTA101 --convert-mseed
# skip figures, write mseed only
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --date 2019-01-15 --no-plot --convert-mseed
--date XOR ( --start + --end ) — required
--station — optional restriction (default: all 3 PREST)
--nc-dir , --plot-dir , --mseed-dir — path overrides
--no-plot — skip figures
--convert-mseed — also write MiniSEED
If we ever want the generated MiniSEED to be ingested by SeedLink or miniseed2dmc, override --mseed-dir to the main pipeline output ( output/mseed/ or output/mseed2dmc/<YEAR>/ ). Today's default keeps it isolated under output/temporal_anomaly/mseed/ so no pipeline state is affected by offline experiments.
New living doc at Obsidian Vault/COSZO/code migration.md . Captures the plan for replacing the legacy gap detection in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py with the integer-step + true_missing approach. Sections:
§1 / §1b — corrected mental model (both old and new use day-global sample rate; per-segment is not changing) + end-to-end pipeline walkthrough tagging every step as 🟥 affected / 🟨 indirectly affected / ⬜ unaffected.
§2 — refined algorithm: replace wall-clock check (param-file dependent) with true_missing = n_ideal − n_points (data-derived).
§3 — risks and edge cases.
§4 — phased plan: Phase 0 (investigator refactor) → Phase 0b (side-by-side comparison) → Phase 1 (extract detect_gaps_{legacy,anomaly} ) → Phase 2 (decisions) → Phase 3 (canary cutover, AXBS first) → Phase 4 (cleanup, includes removing pipeline's save_netcdf ).
§5 — open questions / decisions log with checkboxes.
✓ Splitting trigger : Option A — split only when true_missing > 0 . Jitter-only days produce one MiniSEED for the full day. (Pending William sign-off during Phase 3 canary.)
✓ Sample rate source : Δt_true (OLS slope) used as the day's sampling_rate .
✓ NetCDF saving : investigator-only (via --save-nc ); pipeline's save_netcdf to be removed in Phase 4. Investigator now adopts the server-provided filename convention.
✓ Instability flag : jitter_unstable = (frac_maxabs > 0.4) — sample-rate-agnostic (40 % of Δt_true ). CSV-only diagnostic, no email.
✓ Email policy : keep only sp_deviation as the algorithm-related email (redefined against Δt_true ). 6 upstream pipeline emails unchanged. Jitter instability does not trigger email.
Action on jitter_unstable days beyond the CSV flag (warn-and-write, refuse to write, or fall back to legacy median).
Whether true_missing > 0 should also trigger an email.

Stats text now surfaces true_missing and jitter_unstable .
Suptitle no longer shows sp_nominal ; Δt_true printed at full repr() precision (15–17 significant figures) going forward.
Ran the investigator on the same dates the pre-Phase-0 archive in commit f4196b4 covers, then ran the same range a year ahead (2026) for clean-week behaviour. Both runs without --save-nc ; 2026 with --only-gaps , 2025 without (so we kept all the figures).
| Date | n_points | n_ideal | gap_total_missing (old) | true_missing (new) | n_gaps_raw | jitter_unstable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-22 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 0 | False |
| 2025-01-23 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 0 | False |
| 2025-01-24 | 85238 | 86400 | 1162 | 1162 | 3 | False |
| 2025-01-25 | 84396 | 86400 | 2004 | 2004 | 37 | False |
| 2025-01-26 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 1 (jitter) | False — frac_maxabs = 0.349 , just under 0.4 |
Real-gap days match exactly. Jitter-only day (26) classified as no-gap by both, with the new instability flag False because a single 349 ms residual sat just below the 40 % threshold. Threshold validated.
| Metric | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| n_points | 85308 | |
| n_ideal | 86401 | |
| true_missing | 1093 | n_ideal − n_points |
| n_gaps_raw | 13 | Δi > 1 events |
| gap_total_missing_raw | 1103 | Σ(Δi − 1) over those 13 events |
Discrepancy of 10. The legacy algorithm reports 1103 missing (overcount); the new algorithm reports the actual 1093. The difference is jitter intervals that rounded down to Δi=0 elsewhere in the day, compensating for over-rounded gap events. Same pattern on SUM1 2025-01-25 (1809 raw vs 1807 actual — off by 2).
This is the substantive correctness improvement of the new algorithm: it counts samples that are actually missing, not the apparent count from gap events.
5 days × 3 stations = 15 day-stations, all true_missing = 0 .
0 figures generated ( --only-gaps correctly suppressed all of them on the clean week).
CSV rows still recorded with figure_generated = False .
One worth flagging: SUM1 2026-01-24 had 18 raw Δi>1 events but true_missing = 0 with 86401 points. Old absolute-threshold pipeline would split that day into 19 MiniSEEDs; new Option-A logic keeps it as one. Best validation case in the 2026 batch for the splitting decision.
CSVs: 10 rows per station (5 from 2025 + 5 from 2026).
Figures: 15 dirs from 2025 (full coverage); 0 from 2026 (clean week + --only-gaps ).
Estimate: ~12 000 day-stations × ~50 s per OOI fetch ≈ 150–170 hours of wall time (6–7 days continuous). collect_mode is idempotent — already-processed (station, date) pairs are skipped on resume — so chunking by year keeps progress safe across interruptions.
[ -n "$OOI_USERNAME" ] && [ -n "$OOI_TOKEN" ] && echo "creds set" || source .ooi_env
nohup bash -c '
for year in 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026; do
 echo "=== $year start: $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) ==="
 conda run -n ooi_env python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py \
 --mode collect \
 --start ${year}-01-01 --end ${year}-12-31 \
 --only-gaps
 echo "=== $year end: $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) ==="
done
' > /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log 2>&1 &
echo "PID: $!"
disown
tail -f /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log
wc -l output/temporal_anomaly/metrics/*.csv
pgrep -af temporal_anomaly_investigator
ls output/temporal_anomaly/figures/per_day/ | wc -l
pkill -TERM -f 'temporal_anomaly_investigator.py' # graceful — finishes current day
# or:
pkill -TERM -f 'collect.*2016' # kill the year loop too
# resume — same command, skips everything already in the CSVs
nohup bash -c '...same loop...' > /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log 2>&1 &
Deployment-boundary day (SLBS / SUM1, 2018) may produce a garbage row because a single 24 h window can straddle 15 s → 1 s rates. Δt_FG lands between the two and the reconstruction breaks. Watch for one bad day around each transition; re-investigate manually after the bulk run.
OOI outages turn affected days into has_data=False rows. After the run, find them with awk -F, '$4=="False"' output/temporal_anomaly/metrics/*.csv and re-run that subset.
Disk projection : CSVs ~5 MB total; figures ~5 MB per real-gap day × ~600 days ≈ 3 GB. No NetCDFs unless --save-nc is added.
VM (Kozo) alternative: swap conda run -n ooi_env python for /home/coszo/miniconda3/envs/ooi_env/bin/python /home/coszo/coszo-data-collection/... . VM has ~10 GB free; figures would fit, NetCDFs might not.
Sanity check first : run a single noisy year before committing to the full span:
nohup conda run -n ooi_env python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py \
 --mode collect --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-12-31 --only-gaps \
 > /tmp/collect_2019.log 2>&1 &
disown
That's ~14 hours and gives a feel for OOI's actual response time before the full 11-year run.
Going forward, when running collect_mode :
Always use --save-nc so the local NetCDF archive grows alongside the CSVs (the investigator is the canonical place to save NetCDFs after migration; the pipeline will stop saving them).
Always use --only-gaps so figures are produced only when true_missing > 0 . Clean and jitter-only days get a CSV row with figure_generated=False and no figure directory.
Concretely: the standard collect invocation is
python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py --mode collect \
 --start <YYYY-MM-DD> --end <YYYY-MM-DD> --save-nc --only-gaps
The big-run command above omits --save-nc only because of the disk hit (~12 000 NetCDFs). For smaller, targeted ranges always include --save-nc .
Phase 0 commit 7f961c0 .
code migration.md is the canonical place for migration decisions — refer to it rather than this note for ongoing planning.
